title: LRIM: a Physics-Based Benchmark for Provably Evaluating Long-Range Capabilities in Graph Learning
claim: A physical lattice configuration maps onto a graph learning task whose targets depend on long-range interactions, shown with representative samples.
layout: 3 parts, left-to-right: grid, graph, 2x4 sample heatmaps
description: The figure has three parts, read left to right. On the left is a 4x4 grid of black and white cells. Each cell is marked with a + or − sign to show an Ising spin. In the middle is the same configuration drawn as a lattice graph. Circles with + or − signs are nodes joined by black edges, and the edges run off the edges of the grid. On the right is a 2x4 mosaic of square dot-matrix images. Their captions alternate between 'Input Spins' and 'Target ΔE'. The input spins are purple and yellow dots, mostly yellow in some panels and mostly purple in others. The target energy maps use a yellow-to-purple-to-orange gradient and show smooth, non-trivial structure. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps on the right.
caption: A 4 × 4 Ising spin configuration (left) is represented as an attributed graph (middle) in the LRIM Graph Benchmark. (Right) Four representative 32x32 spin configurations from the LRIM32 dataset and their corresponding ∆E energy landscapes, demonstrating the non-trivial energetic landscape which provably depends on long-range interactions.
abstract: Accurately modeling long-range dependencies in graph-structured data is critical for many real-world applications. However, incorporating long-range interactions beyond the nodes' immediate neighborhood in a $\textit{scalable}$ manner remains an open challenge for graph machine learning models. Existing benchmarks for evaluating long-range capabilities either cannot $\textit{guarantee}$ that their tasks actually depend on long-range information or are rather limited. Therefore, claims of long-range modeling improvements based on said performance remain questionable. We introduce the Long-Range Ising Model Graph Benchmark, a physics-based benchmark utilizing the well-studied Ising model whose ground truth $\textit{provably}$ depends on long-range dependencies. Our benchmark consists of ten datasets that scale from 256 to 65k nodes per graph, and provide controllable long-range dependencies through tunable parameters, allowing precise control over the hardness and ``long-rangedness". We provide model-agnostic evidence that local information is insufficient, further validating the design choices of our benchmark. Via experiments on classical message-passing architectures and graph transformers, we show that both perform far from the optimum, especially those with scalable complexity. Our goal is that our benchmark will foster the development of scalable methodologies that effectively model long-range interactions in graphs.
